title: AQA GCSE Physics · Atomic Structure and Radiation (part 2)

items.stem: Which statement about background radiation is correct?

options.text: It is around us all of the time, from natural and from man-made sources.
It is present only in an area that a nuclear accident has affected.
It exists only because people have built reactors and weapons.
It is found only in places where uranium-bearing rock lies.

items.why: Background radiation is continuously present, and it has both natural sources such as rocks and cosmic rays from space and man-made sources such as fallout.

items.stem: Which of these is a natural source of background radiation?

options.text: Fallout still present from earlier nuclear weapons tests
Cosmic rays that reach the Earth's surface from space
Radioactive waste kept in a store at a power plant
Radiation produced by an X-ray machine in a hospital

items.why: Cosmic rays from space are named in the specification as a natural source of background radiation, alongside rocks.

items.stem: An accident at a nuclear power station releases radioactive material that settles over nearby farmland. How should this contribution to the background radiation there be classified?

options.text: As natural, because the isotopes also occur in rocks
As natural, since the fallout now lies in soil
As man-made, because human activity released it
As neither, because the material has spread widely

items.why: The specification lists the fallout from nuclear accidents as a man-made source; the classification depends on origin, not on where the material ends up.

items.stem: Which pair are both man-made sources of background radiation?

options.text: Cosmic rays from space and rocks lying in the earth
Rocks in the ground and waste from nuclear accidents
Cosmic rays from space and fallout from weapons tests
Fallout from weapons testing and nuclear accidents

items.why: These are exactly the two man-made sources named in the specification.

items.stem: A radiographer in a hospital records a higher annual radiation dose than an office worker who lives in the same street. What is the best explanation?

options.text: Everyone receives the same dose, so the readings must be faulty.
Her occupation exposes her to radiation that the office worker never meets.
Radiation collects in the body of anybody who works indoors all day.
Both really get equal doses, so the extra reading must come from the building.

items.why: The specification states that radiation dose may be affected by occupation; work with X-ray equipment and radioactive sources adds to her dose.

items.stem: People living where the local rock is granite, and aircrew who fly long-haul routes, both receive above-average annual radiation doses. Which statement explains both cases?

options.text: Fallout from nuclear weapons tests gathers on high ground and on granite.
The aircrew's height should lower their dose, so only the granite case is real.
Location affects dose: granite gives radon, altitude gives cosmic rays.
Everyone really gets the same dose, so both averages must be wrong.

items.why: The specification states that the level of background radiation may be affected by location; radon from rock and cosmic rays are both natural sources whose level varies with where you are.

items.stem: A safety leaflet states that a worker received a radiation dose of 4.5 mSv during one year. What does this dose value describe?

options.text: The number of counts that her detector recorded each second.
The number of nuclei that decayed in the sources she used.
The mass of radioactive material she took into her body.
The risk of harm to her body from the radiation absorbed.

items.why: Radiation dose measures the risk of harm to body tissue from the radiation absorbed; it depends on the amount and the type of radiation.

items.stem: A patient's total radiation dose over a course of treatment is 2500 mSv. Using 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv), what is this dose in sieverts?

options.text: 2.5 Sv

items.why: A millisievert is one thousandth of a sievert, so 2500 mSv is divided by 1000, giving 2.5 Sv.

items.stem: A worker's badge records a dose of 45 mSv over one year. Using 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv), what is this dose in sieverts?

options.text: 45 Sv
4.5 Sv

items.why: 45 mSv divided by 1000 gives 0.045 Sv, correctly a smaller number than the value in millisieverts.

items.stem: Which statement about the half-life values of radioactive isotopes is correct?

options.text: They are all much the same, since every unstable nucleus decays at a similar rate.
They all lie between a few seconds and a few days, for any isotope at all.
They change with the temperature and the pressure a sample is kept at.
They cover a very wide range, from fractions of a second to billions of years.

items.why: The specification states that radioactive isotopes have a very wide range of half-life values.

items.stem: A radioactive isotope with a half-life of many thousands of years is spilled onto open ground. Why is such a long half-life a particular hazard here?

options.text: The ground stays radioactive for a very long time after the spill.
Its activity is enormous, so it emits a great deal of radiation now.
Isotopes with a long half-life always emit alpha, the worst kind of all.
It decays so fast that it spreads over the whole area at once.

items.why: A long half-life means the activity falls only very slowly, so the contamination remains a hazard for generations.

items.stem: A source with a half-life of a few minutes is spilled in a school laboratory. Why is it a serious hazard at once but much less of one an hour later?

options.text: The nuclei all stop decaying once one half-life has gone by.
Its activity is high at first and then falls away fast.
A short half-life means it gives out no radiation at all.
Its radiation changes from gamma into harmless alpha rays.

items.why: A short half-life means very many decays each second at the start, and that rate halves every few minutes, so the hazard is immediate but brief.

items.stem: A tracer is injected so that a doctor can watch how a patient's kidneys are working. Which property makes an isotope suitable for this use?

options.text: It emits alpha radiation, which is easily detected through the skin.
It has a half-life of many years, so the scan could be repeated later.
It emits radiation intense enough to destroy the tissue it reaches.
It emits gamma radiation, which leaves the body and is detected outside.

items.why: Gamma radiation is penetrating and weakly ionising, so it passes out to a detector while depositing comparatively little energy in the patient.

items.stem: How are nuclear radiations used to control or destroy a tumour lying deep inside the body?

options.text: A high dose of gamma radiation is aimed at the tumour from outside.
A weak alpha source is swallowed and travels to the tumour site itself.
A gamma source is placed so precisely that it harms only the tumour and nothing else.
The tumour is cooled by radiation until its cells stop dividing.

items.why: External beam radiotherapy uses a high dose of penetrating gamma radiation directed at the tumour, often rotated around the patient.

items.stem: A gamma-emitting tracer with a half-life of about six hours is chosen instead of one with a half-life of several years. Evaluate this choice.

options.text: Poor: a source that decays this quickly cannot give out enough radiation to be detected.
Good: the activity falls quickly, so the patient's dose after the scan stays small.
It makes no difference: once inside, you stay radioactive for life whatever the half-life.
Poor: a longer-lived tracer would let the doctors scan the same organ again later.

items.why: A half-life of hours gives ample activity for imaging and then decays away, limiting the dose received once the scan is over.

items.stem: A scan using a radioactive tracer gives a patient a dose of about 6 mSv. The average annual dose from background radiation is about 2.7 mSv. The patient refuses the scan, saying that any nuclear radiation is too dangerous. Which is the best evaluation of that decision?

options.text: Refusing is right: even a dose no bigger than background must be avoided.
Refusing is right, because man-made radiation harms the body more than background.
The small added risk should be weighed against the benefit of a diagnosis.
Refusing is right, since a dose above background is certain to cause a cancer.

items.why: Evaluating a perceived risk against given data means comparing a dose of a few millisieverts with the consequences of leaving an illness undiagnosed.

items.stem: A gamma beam rotated around a patient destroys a deep tumour, but it also passes through healthy tissue. Evaluate this treatment.

options.text: Justified: the tumour is destroyed and the dose to healthy tissue is limited.
Ideal: careful aiming means that only the tumour receives any radiation.
Unjustified: no dose of nuclear radiation to a patient is acceptable.
Ineffective: gamma is too weakly ionising to damage a deep tumour.

items.why: Rotating the beam spreads the dose to healthy tissue over a large volume while the tumour stays in the path, so the benefit outweighs the side effects.

items.stem: Which statement describes nuclear fission?

options.text: The joining of two light nuclei into a single heavier nucleus.
The breaking of a nucleus into its separate protons and neutrons.
The splitting of a small, stable nucleus such as a carbon nucleus.
The splitting of a large, unstable nucleus such as a uranium nucleus.

items.why: This is the specification's definition: fission is the splitting of a large and unstable nucleus, eg uranium or plutonium.

items.stem: A power station uses uranium as its fuel. Why can a uranium nucleus undergo fission when a carbon nucleus cannot?

options.text: A carbon nucleus can be split just as easily as a uranium one.
A uranium nucleus is large and unstable, so it can split.
A uranium atom holds more electrons than a carbon atom.
A carbon nucleus can only join to others, never split.

items.why: Fission is the splitting of a large and unstable nucleus, eg uranium or plutonium; a small stable nucleus such as carbon does not undergo fission.

items.stem: Spontaneous fission is rare. What must usually happen before a large unstable nucleus undergoes fission?

options.text: The unstable nucleus must first absorb a neutron.
The unstable nucleus must be heated to a high temperature.
The unstable nucleus must first absorb a proton.
The unstable nucleus must first absorb a gamma ray.

items.why: The specification states that usually, for fission to occur, the unstable nucleus must first absorb a neutron.

items.stem: A uranium nucleus absorbs a neutron and undergoes fission. Apart from gamma rays, what does the fission produce?

options.text: Two smaller nuclei of about the same size, and a single extra neutron.
One large nucleus and one very small nucleus, plus a few free neutrons.
Two smaller nuclei of roughly equal size, plus two or three neutrons.
A shower of individual protons and neutrons from the nucleus that split.

items.why: The nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei, roughly equal in size, and emits two or three neutrons plus gamma rays.

items.stem: A uranium nucleus undergoes fission. Which statement about the two nuclei it produces is correct?

options.text: They are stable, so no further radiation is ever emitted by them.
They are roughly equal in size, and both are smaller than the uranium nucleus.
One is much larger than the other, and the smaller is a proton.
One keeps almost all the mass, and the other is only a tiny fragment.

items.why: The nucleus undergoing fission splits into two smaller nuclei, roughly equal in size.

items.stem: In a fission event, which of the products are given kinetic energy?

options.text: Only the two smaller nuclei that are formed by the split.
None of them, since the energy is carried off by the gamma rays.
Only the neutrons, which then go on to cause more fission.
All of them, including each of the neutrons that are emitted.

items.why: The specification states that all of the fission products have kinetic energy.

items.stem: Why can a single fission event lead to a chain reaction?

options.text: The gamma rays given out are absorbed by other nuclei, making those split too.
The energy released heats the fuel up until the nuclei around it break apart.
The neutrons released are absorbed by other nuclei, making those split too.
One neutron comes out, which splits exactly one more nucleus.

items.why: The neutrons emitted may go on to start a chain reaction: each absorbed neutron can cause a further fission.

items.stem: How does the chain reaction inside a nuclear reactor differ from the one in a nuclear weapon?

options.text: In the reactor it is controlled; in the weapon it is not.
The reactor releases energy slowly because it uses a different fuel.
The reactor splits nuclei, while the weapon works by joining them.
The weapon uses a chain reaction, but the reactor does not use one.

items.why: The chain reaction is controlled in a nuclear reactor to control the energy released, whereas the weapon's explosion is caused by an uncontrolled chain reaction.

items.stem: The chain reaction in a nuclear reactor is controlled. What does controlling it achieve?

options.text: It keeps the rate of fission steady, so the energy is released steadily.
It stops the chain reaction, so that no further fission takes place.
It makes the reaction spread faster, so more energy is given out.
It removes the gamma rays produced, so no radiation escapes.

items.why: The chain reaction is controlled in a nuclear reactor to control the energy released, so the core delivers energy steadily instead of all at once.

items.stem: A student is drawing a chain reaction diagram. One neutron causes a fission that releases three neutrons, and each of those is absorbed by another uranium nucleus. What should the diagram show next?

options.text: One further fission, with the two spare neutrons simply stopping there.
Three further fissions, each of them releasing three more neutrons.
Three further fissions, each of them releasing one new neutron.
Three bursts of gamma radiation spreading out from the nuclei.

items.why: Each absorbed neutron causes a fission that emits two or three neutrons of its own, so the diagram branches: one, then three, then nine.

items.stem: Which statement describes nuclear fusion?

options.text: Two heavy nuclei join together to form one lighter nucleus.
A large unstable nucleus splits into two fragments.
Two light nuclei join to form a single heavier nucleus.
Two atoms bond together to make a molecule with one nucleus.

items.why: Nuclear fusion is the joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus.

items.stem: Two light nuclei fuse to form a heavier nucleus. What may happen to some of their mass?

options.text: It is thrown out of the new nucleus as extra neutrons.
It stays the same, since mass is always conserved.
It is used up in splitting the new nucleus apart.
It is converted into the energy of radiation.

items.why: In this process some of the mass may be converted into the energy of radiation.
